result:
At 4:17 in the afternoon, the city briefly forgot what it was doing.

The traffic lights continued their obedient changing, red to green, green to yellow. Buses sighed at the curb. Somewhere, a dog barked at a delivery truck with the unwavering conviction of a prophet. But beneath all this motion, something paused.

A woman standing outside a bakery looked up and saw that one cloud had separated from the others. It was small and silver-edged, shaped almost like a boat. She wondered where it was going.

Inside the bakery, a boy pressed his palm against the glass display. The cakes were arranged in careful rows: chocolate, lemon, strawberry, each one shining under the warm lights. He had been told to choose only one. This seemed to him an impossible responsibility.

On the rooftop across the street, an old man watered a pot of basil. The basil had survived winter, pigeons, heat, and three separate attempts by the wind to carry its soil away. He touched one leaf between his fingers and smiled at the sharp green smell.

No one noticed the city pause. That was the nature of such moments. They did not arrive with bells or announcements. They slipped between footsteps, hid inside the breath before a sentence, waited in the quiet space after a song ended.

Then the traffic light changed.

The woman went into the bakery. The boy chose chocolate. The old man set down his watering can.

And the cloud, carrying nothing anyone could see, sailed on.
